newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: French ban to hit Dutch airfreight truckers.
newsitem.headline: French ban to hit Dutch airfreight truckers.

text.p: Dutch airfreight truckers said the French government's ban on weekend road haulage traffic starting on March 24 was "bad for all hauliers."

A Dutch Transport Association(KNV) spokesman said a major complaint is the uncertainty surrounding whether any special exemptions will be granted under the ban, although it is possible that perishables will be excluded.

Currently, truckers are allowed to return back to their home location. But after the ban comes into force trucks, weighing more than 7.5 tonnes, are banned from the French roads from 10 p.m. (2100 gmt) Friday until the same time on Sunday evening.
Nico Leyer, managing director of one of the leading airfreight truckers in the Netherlands, Rutges BV, said: "We have no real information about the ban, no one seems to be able to give answers."

The KNV spokesman said: "It is no longer certain whether there will be exemptions in place for airfreight haulage. And for general haulage companies it looks like it will be impossible to deliver their cargo.
"There seems to be some special permits for French companies but it is not clear whether these will be available for foreign companies."

Leyer said the company was especially worried for its airfreight and perishables business. "Airlines have schedules, we cannot stop those. What do we do if the cargo is flown in at the weekend? We have to be able to meet the deadlines for the airline industry."
Rutges has approximately 50 trailers passing through France each weekend, he added, with around 40 percent of this cargo being perishable traffic.
Leyer added that the stoppage had implications for traffic between the continent and Britain.

Wim Heeren, managing director of Jan de Rijk, a leading airfreight trucking company, said: "The Dover-Calais truck route and Channel Tunnel route are very heavy routes for us. If we cannot travel through France at the weekend, what are the implications for the UK economy?"
A spokesman for Nedlloyd Road Cargo commented: "We will have a problem with cargo for Spain and Portugal."
KLM Cargo announced recently that it would be starting a week-end freighter service to Zaragoza because of the French trucking ban.
The KNV spokesman said: "It seems we will have the same system as in Germany when the trucks have to wait alongside the roads until the ban ends."

He said KNV has advised its members, who total 9,000 operators and 35 percent of all vehicles in the Netherlands, to apply for exemption permits and if they had problems to immediately contact the association.
Then he would decide whether to go straight to the French Ministry of Transport or to take up the matter with the European transport commissioner, Neil Kinnock.
